source_text:
Refractory high‐entropy alloys (RHEA, also called multi‐principal‐element refractory alloys) comprise five or more principal elements from the refractory transition metals (group 4–6 elements: Zr, Hf, V, Nb, Ta, Mo, and W, often with Ti and Cr also considered), with structural applications under extreme temperature conditions, beyond those where nickel‐based superalloys can be used. Additive manufacturing (AM) of RHEAs can facilitate the exploration of possible applications for RHEA via rapid prototyping of parts with complex shapes with high powder feedstock utilization. Recently, laser melting deposition (LMD) was used to fabricate NbTaTiZr, HfNbTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, and MoNbTaW quaternary and quinary refractory concentrated alloys. However, the feature resolution of LMD is relatively low, as the size of the melt pool is as large as ≈3 mm. In addition, no complex parts have been demonstrated for these refractory alloys by using LMD. Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is another additive manufacturing method that was used to fabricate MoNbTaVW and MoNbTaX (X = Ti, Ni, Ti0.5Ni0.5) refractory alloys. However, cracking usually occurs from significant thermal stresses caused by the very fast cooling rate during the solidification of the melt pool.

An alternate AM method is 3D ink‐extrusion printing (material extrusion), which can extrude powder‐loaded inks, layer by layer, at room temperature to fabricate complex green parts with micro‐features, which are then densified by sintering. Isothermal sintering allows for very low thermal stresses preventing the associated cracking observed in LPBF. Also, sintered microstructures have no crystallographic texture, unlike LMD or LPBF alloys. Another advantage is that the printability of the ink depends solely on its rheology and does not necessitate the spherical shape and large powder sizes required for powder‐bed‐based AM methods, including binder jetting. Furthermore, atomization of alloyed powders can be avoided by using elemental powder blends, and rapid sintering can be achieved by using fine powders with irregular shapes. Previously, 3D ink‐extrusion printing has successfully fabricated strong and ductile equiatomic lower‐melting alloys such as CoCrFeNi, CoCrCuFeNi, and CoCrFeMnNi HEA microlattices, using elemental or prealloyed powders. We are not aware of any published work on 3D ink‐extrusion printing of RHEA, except for Zhao et al. who used 3D ink‐extrusion printing to fabricate equiatomic NbTaTiZr scaffolds, which showed good biocompatibility and met the requirements for orthopedic implants.

In the cast state, equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr shows good tensile ductility at room temperature (8–16%) and excellent strength at high temperatures (e.g., yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C for strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1). However, the poor oxygen resistance of HfNbTaTiZr prevents most practical applications at high temperatures. Coating with stable oxide formers (e.g., Al, Si, and Cr) is often used to improve the oxidation resistance of alloys: for example, Saad et al. coated Hf0.5Nb0.5Ta0.5Ti1.5Zr with an aluminide layer, which prevented the pesting behavior (disintegration into powders) when exposed to air at 800 °C for 5 h. To our knowledge, silicide coatings have not been studied for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, but they have been used to coat MoNbTaW, MoNbTaVW, and AlMo0.5NbTa0.5TiZr; they have the advantage of forming a dense SiO2‐rich scale during oxidation, which can flow and heal cracks at elevated temperatures.

queries.broad: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.
queries.problem_constrained: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.
queries.expert_context: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr combines room-temperature ductility with high-temperature strength, but poor oxygen resistance restricts its use. Fabrication studies on refractory concentrated alloys have also encountered limitations: laser melting deposition has a melt-pool size of about 3 mm and has not demonstrated complex refractory-alloy parts, while laser powder bed fusion commonly produces cracking because rapid cooling generates large thermal stresses. Prior oxidation work used stable-oxide-forming coatings: an aluminide layer prevented pesting of Hf0.5Nb0.5Ta0.5Ti1.5Zr during 5 h in air at 800 °C, while silicide coatings that form dense, crack-healing SiO2-rich scales were demonstrated on other refractory alloys rather than equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr. Subject to the design constraints of producing complex micro-featured parts, limiting thermally induced cracking and crystallographic texture, and retaining useful mechanical properties, what single intervention should be hypothesized to improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr? Specify its mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the untreated alloy, operating boundaries, supporting evidence from the cited earlier work, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

queries.expert_context: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.
